newsitem.title: FRANCE: Competition tough in Euro appliances - French report.
newsitem.headline: Competition tough in Euro appliances - French report.

text.p: European appliance makers face an onslaught of competition from U.S. and Asian manufacturers attracted by the size of the European market and high disposable income, France's Industry Ministry said on Tuesday.

"We're observing a significant rise in competition in Europe...with Chinese sales up 400 percent in the small appliance segment in less than 10 years," it said in a report on the industry. Chinese manufacturers have captured more than half the sales in Europe of toasters and hair dryers, it said.
France's large appliance manufacturers have been taken over by other European companies but it boasts two big names in small appliances, Moulinex and SEB.
SEB generates two-thirds of its sales outside France and Moulinex three-quarters, but they are feeling pressure from competition as well as slow growth in their main markets.
SEB is holding up well but Moulinex lost money last year and plans to close two French plants, cutting more than 2,000 jobs.
On Tuesday, Sweden's Electrolux reported a 14 percent drop in first-quarter earnings.
European companies still control 85 percent of their market, but manufacturers from other regions are coming into Europe.

"Among them, Korean manufacturers belonging to financially powerful conglomerates are setting up new facilities," notably in Britain and in the northeastern French region of Lorraine, said the report prepared by the ministry's industrial statistics division.
Daewoo Electronics, for instance, makes microwave ovens in France.
U.S. groups have long targeted Europe, led by Whirlpool, which bought Philips' small appliance business in 1989, and General Electric Co, the report said.

"Some companies, such as Whirlpool of the United States and the Koreans, are pushing the market toward homogeneity and seek to propose a standard for each product. In contrast, the Europeans Electrolux, Bosch-Siemens and Brandt (a unit of Italy's Elfi), are opting for differentiation," it said.
The report said the appliance industry was among the most sensitive to exchange rate fluctuations.

It noted that tastes and habits varied from one country to the next and had a big impact on demand. Electric kettles are big sellers in Britain and Russia but not in France, blenders are more popular in northern Europe than in the Mediterranean, washing machines are bigger in the United States and consume much more water, and U.S. refrigerators are also much bigger.

Italians do not buy as many clothes dryers as other Europeans. French people like to load washers from the top, and Germans from the front. Microwave ovens, big sellers everywhere, are the exception to the rule, the report said.
